query: Prior studies of Al-containing Cr–Co–Fe–Ni alloys showed that composition and thermal history can substantially alter constituent phases and transformation behavior, but they did not establish a predictive explanation of phase stability across the relevant thermal regime or adequately connect it to composition-dependent thermodynamic instability. Given the competing thermodynamic and kinetic factors in multicomponent alloys, what single testable mechanistic hypothesis explains what governs phase stability in Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 initially in a high-temperature BCC state and why? State a controlled comparison and baseline, predicted observations, boundary conditions, prior evidence supporting the hypothesis, and a result that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: In Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 initially stabilized in a high-temperature BCC state, strong Al–Ni and Al–Fe chemical interactions induce partial B2-type ordering within the BCC lattice upon cooling, governed by the balance of thermodynamic driving forces for ordering and the extent of diffusional mobility at intermediate temperatures. Rapid cooling suppresses this transformation, freezing in the high-temperature BCC state and indicating a kinetic origin of the ordering.
generation.material_initial_state: A homogenized Cr39Co18Fe18Ni18Al7 alloy with a single-phase BCC structure obtained by solution treatment at high temperature.
generation.intervention: Monitor the alloy during continuous cooling or isothermal holds (850–1000 °C) using in situ synchrotron or neutron diffraction to capture real-time development of B2-like ordering in the BCC matrix.
generation.conditions: Apply multiple cooling rates (e.g., 1 K/min vs. 20 K/min) and hold times up to 24 h to systematically vary diffusion kinetics and maintain comparable bulk composition and existing microstructure prior to cooling.
generation.structural_mediator: Formation of Al-rich B2-ordered domains within the disordered BCC phase driven by local Al–TM short-range order.
generation.mechanism: Energetically favorable Al–Ni/Al–Fe interactions reduce the free energy when forming B2-ordered clusters. The interplay between thermodynamic instability of the high-temperature BCC phase and diffusional measures at intermediate temperatures drives B2 precipitation; faster cooling curtails diffusion and inhibits ordering.
generation.predicted_outcome: (1) B2-type ordered domains emerge upon slow or intermediate cooling, manifesting as distinct superlattice diffraction peaks. (2) Rapid quenching prevents observable B2 formation, leaving the high-temperature BCC state intact. (3) Extended isothermal exposure near 850–1000 °C enhances B2 domain coarsening.
generation.baseline: A compositionally similar alloy with reduced Al content, predicted to exhibit diminished or delayed B2 formation under identical thermal processing, due to less pronounced Al-driven ordering tendencies.
generation.boundary: Above ~1100 °C, the BCC matrix remains fully disordered; extremely fast cooling (<20 K/s) or near-zero cooling rates can generate out-of-equilibrium or competing phases, complicating interpretation of B2 formation.
generation.uncertainty: Specific onset temperatures and growth kinetics of B2 domains may shift if additional Cr–Ni or Fe–Cr interactions compete with Al–Ni/Al–Fe ordering pathways.

falsification_experiment.design: Perform time-resolved diffraction measurements of samples cooled from 1200 °C at varying rates and held isothermally at 900 °C to capture the evolution of B2 reflections in situ.
measurements: Intensity and positions of B2 (superlattice) diffraction peaks across the cooling trajectory and during isothermal holds.
Compositional profiles (via EDS or other mapping) around B2 precipitates before and after heat treatments.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If no ordered reflections appear at moderate cooling rates and relevant hold temperatures, or if B2 formation is not suppressed by rapid quenching, the hypothesis is invalidated.

cited_evidence.kind: web:Phase selection in solid-state phase transformation process
cited_evidence.text: Besides the rapid solidification, the effects of solid-state transformation kinetics on the phase selection were investigated via different cooling rate after annealing the CoCrFeNiTi0.4 HEA at 900 °C and 1080 °C. The corresponding SEM images are presented in Fig. 4. It shows that, when the CoCrFeNiTi0.4 HEA was annealed at 1080 °C and quenched in water (Q1, Fig. 4(a)), only a small amount of platelet-like phase can be found. However, plenty of nano-particles and platelet-like phases showed up when the sample was cooled in the heat treatment furnace (FC1, Fig. 4(b)). The XRD results, as shown in Fig. 2, indicated that Q1 HEA had mainly FCC phase and minor Laves and R phases while the FC1 HEA was composed of γ′, R, σ, Laves and FCC phases. These results illustrated that a high cooling rate during the solid-state phase transformation can prevent the precipitation of γ′ and σ phases.

cited_evidence.text: Based on the preceding results, the kinetic effect in CoCrFeNiTi0.4 HEA can be concluded. The cooling rate of LR HEA is the highest, thus R, σ and γ′ phases are all inhibited in this condition; with the decrease of cooling rate, the R phase shows up in an AC sample. As for the solid-state transformation process, the cooling rate of the Q1 HEA is quite high, and σ phase was restrained under the rapid quenching condition. And actually, the γ′ phase is also inhibited when quenched in water. All the phases can be formed when the cooling rate is sufficiently low, which is similar to the equilibrium condition. The FC1 sample in this study proved this conclusion. If the phases occurred during annealing at the corresponding temperature, as the Q2 and FC2 shown, the cooling rate would not affect the phase selection. Utilizing this kinetic effect, tailoring phases in HEAs can be realized. Figure 5(a) presented the equilibrium phase diagram of the CoCrFeNiTi0.4 HEA obtained by thermodynamic calculations. decision.trend: Early work (PMC6207727) used first-principles and Monte Carlo simulations to capture phase evolution in Al-containing Cr–Co–Fe–Ni alloys, enabling semi-quantitative predictions across temperatures. However, subsequent efforts to apply CALPHAD (PMC7512484) revealed data gaps and inaccuracies in extrapolating phase equilibria for highly concentrated systems. More recent computational studies (PMC7927031, PMC12177746) focused on atomic interactions and enthalpies of mixing in multi-principal element alloys, improving predictions of structural stability but still leaving open questions about reconciling kinetic effects and short-range order with thermodynamics. Even as modeling expanded to incorporate multi-scale interactions, a unifying explanation that robustly predicts how composition-driven instabilities yield specific transformations remains incomplete.
decision.unsolved: It remains unclear precisely how local Al-driven short-range order and competing diffusion kinetics collectively govern the stability and transformation pathways of high-temperature BCC Al–Cr–Co–Fe–Ni alloys. While theory suggests that strong Al–Ni and Al–Fe interactions can favor ordered B2-like domains, tying these observations to thermodynamic instability and tracing how transformations proceed over relevant time–temperature regimes has not been conclusively demonstrated.
decision.lever: Conduct time-resolved in situ synchrotron or neutron diffraction during controlled cooling from the high-temperature BCC state, focusing on the emergence of Al-rich B2 ordering. Vary the cooling rate (e.g., 1 K/min vs. 20 K/min) and intermediate hold times (e.g., up to 24 h at 850–1000 °C). Track lattice parameters and diffraction peak splitting as transformation proceeds in real time.
decision.why: By directly monitoring ordering and precipitation on relevant timescales, one can test the mechanistic hypothesis that strong Al–Ni/Al–Fe interactions drive site-specific ordering in the BCC matrix, creating B2-like clusters at intermediate temperatures when diffusion is sufficient to allow partial chemical segregation. If the B2 ordering initiates at the predicted temperature–time conditions and coexists with a diminishing disordered BCC phase (and is suppressed by rapid quenching), it confirms the role of composition-driven thermodynamic instability and kinetic modulation in determining phase stability. If no distinct ordering onset is observed or the transformation sequence follows an unpredicted pathway, the mechanistic hypothesis is falsified.
